content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.8. I used the full budget of 60.

**Design:** I trained the learner on 8 tasks. Three rules (L1, S1, M1) each appeared in at least 3 of them, and two rules (L2, S4) appeared in only one. Before training, I used the free `compare` command to choose test tasks where how new the rules are and how similar the task is to trained ones point in different directions.

| Test task | New rules | Max similarity to trained | Mean examples (n) |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M3 (already trained) | 0 | 1.0 | 14.5 (6) |
| L1-S1-M4 | 1 | 0.75 | 13.0 (8) |
| L1-S1-M1 (each rule seen 3+ times) | 0 | 0.375 | 29.3 (12) |
| L2-S4-M1 (two rules seen once) | 0 | 0.375 | 29.9 (9) |
| L2-S2-M2 | 1 | 0.25 | 42.7 (7) |

**Why holistic:**
- **Against part-based:** L1-S1-M4 and L2-S2-M2 each have one new rule, but their costs differ by more than 3×, and the difference follows similarity. L1-S1-M4 also cost about the same as a task the learner was already trained on, even though it has a new rule.
- **Against factor-when-justified:** L1-S1-M1 should have been cheap under this hypothesis, because all its rules had appeared in at least 3 trained tasks and so would have become reusable parts. It cost the same as L2-S4-M1, whose rules hadn't appeared often enough to become parts and which had equal similarity. This holds whether k is 2 or 3.
- **For holistic:** cost rises steadily as similarity falls, and doesn't depend on how new the rules are or how often they were trained.

**Caveat:** the noise is very large. Single samples of the same task ranged from 1 to 52. The A-vs-B comparison is the main evidence against factor-when-justified, and with about 10 samples per task it could miss a small benefit from reusable parts. That's why the confidence is 0.8 rather than higher.
